title: Kings of the North and South
summary: The messenger reveals a long sequence of conflicts: Persian kings, a mighty Greek king whose empire is broken into four, and generations of wars between the king of the South and the king of the North, with the Beautiful Land caught between them. A despicable king of the North rises, attacks the holy covenant, abolishes the daily sacrifice, and sets up the abomination of desolation, while those who know their God stand firm and the wise teach many, even at the cost of their lives. The chapter closes with the king exalting himself above every god and meeting his end with no one to help him.
story: This is the heart of the final vision introduced in chapter 10. The messenger said he would tell Daniel what is written in the Book of Truth (10:21), and now he does, in more detail than any other prophecy in the Old Testament. The chapter narrows the focus of the earlier visions. Chapter 2 and chapter 7 surveyed a sequence of empires; chapter 8 focused on Persia, Greece, and a little horn; chapter 11 follows the Greek period king by king until it reaches the ruler who attacks God's people and temple. That crisis, and the faithfulness it demands, is where the whole book has been heading. Chapter 12 will give the answer to it: deliverance, resurrection, and a promise to the faithful.
historical:
Most interpreters of every school agree that verses 2-35 match the history of the fourth to second centuries BC closely. Persia will have three more kings and a fourth richer than all, often identified as Xerxes I, who invaded Greece in 480 BC (verse 2). The mighty king is Alexander the Great, whose empire was divided among his generals after his death in 323 BC (verses 3-4). The king of the South is the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt; the king of the North is the Seleucid dynasty in Syria and Mesopotamia. Ptolemy I's commander who grew stronger is Seleucus I (verse 5). The daughter sent north is Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married to Antiochus II around 252 BC and later murdered with her child (verse 6). Her brother Ptolemy III avenged her and carried off Seleucid treasures and images (verses 7-9). Antiochus III, the Great, lost to Ptolemy IV at Raphia in 217 BC (verses 10-12) but won at Panium around 200 BC, bringing Judea under Seleucid rule (verses 13-16). He married his daughter Cleopatra I to Ptolemy V (verse 17), was defeated by the Romans at Magnesia in 190 BC (verse 18), and died in 187 BC (verse 19). His son Seleucus IV sent his minister Heliodorus to seize temple funds (verse 20; 2 Maccabees 3).

The despicable person of verses 21-35 is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who took the throne in 175 BC though he was not the heir. The prince of the covenant (verse 22) is widely identified with the high priest Onias III. Antiochus invaded Egypt in 169 BC and plundered the Jerusalem temple on his return (verses 25-28; 1 Maccabees 1:20-24). On a second campaign in 168 BC a Roman envoy, arriving by ship, ordered him out of Egypt (verses 29-30; Kittim here means the Romans). In 167 BC he banned Jewish worship and set up a pagan altar in the temple (verse 31; 1 Maccabees 1:54). The little help of verse 34 is often taken as the Maccabean revolt.
cultural:
The chapter reflects the politics of the Hellenistic world, the Greek-speaking culture Alexander spread across the Near East. Royal marriages sealed treaties between rival dynasties, and daughters were sent across borders as pledges, often at great personal cost (verses 6 and 17). Conquerors carried off the images of defeated nations' gods to show whose gods were stronger (verse 8), and temple treasuries, including Jerusalem's, were tempting sources of cash for kings paying soldiers and debts. Judea lay on the road between Egypt and Syria, so every war between South and North passed through the Beautiful Land.

The Jewish community under Antiochus was divided. Some leading families welcomed Greek customs, built a gymnasium in Jerusalem, and bought the high priesthood (1 Maccabees 1:11-15; 2 Maccabees 4); these are the ones who forsake or violate the covenant (verses 30, 32). Others refused to abandon the law even under torture and death. The chapter honors the people who know their God and the wise teachers, the maskilim, who instructed many and suffered for it (verses 32-35). The honor belongs to faithfulness, not to military success.
literary: The chapter is written as prophecy in the future tense, but in the veiled style of apocalyptic: no king is named, only titles and roles (king of the South, king of the North, a despicable person, a commander). The repeated pattern of alliance, betrayal, and war gives the history a numbing sameness, as if to show that the empires' struggles go around and around without producing anything lasting. Refrains break the pattern: but it will not succeed, but only for a time, for the end will come at the appointed time (verses 27, 29, 35). These remind the reader that the whole sequence runs on God's schedule. At verse 36 the tone shifts. The king magnifies himself above every god, and verses 40-45 describe a final campaign that does not correspond clearly to known events, which is where the schools of interpretation divide (see the hard question).

outline.t: Persia and the mighty king of Greece
Wars between the kings of the South and the North
The despicable king and his first campaigns
The attack on the holy covenant and the faithful wise
The king who exalts himself above every god
The final campaign and the king's end

doctrines.note: Kings plot, marry, betray, and conquer, but the refrain of the chapter is that the end will come at the appointed time. What has been decreed must be accomplished (verse 36). Human power is real but bounded, and God sets its limits.

The faithful are not promised safety. Some of the wise will fall, so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless (verse 35). Persecution is not a sign that God has lost control; it becomes the fire in which faith is proved.
Against a king who corrupts with flattery, the people who know their God firmly resist him (verse 32). Knowing God is the root of courage under pressure.
The king ends by magnifying himself above every god and honoring a god of fortresses. The chapter exposes the religion of power: a ruler who worships force, wealth, and himself.

words.note: Sakal, to be wise, to have insight, and in some forms to make wise or instruct. Those with insight (the maskilim) instruct many (verse 33), and some of the wise fall (verse 35). In 12:3 they will shine like the brightness of the heavens. The book's heroes are teachers who understand God's ways and help others hold fast.

Maoz, a stronghold or place of refuge. It appears repeatedly in the chapter for fortresses and for the temple fortress Antiochus desecrates (verse 31), and the king finally honors a god of fortresses (verse 38). Elsewhere in the Old Testament the LORD himself is his people's stronghold (Psalm 27:1; Nahum 1:7), which sharpens the contrast.

Berit, covenant. The chapter speaks of the holy covenant (verses 28, 30), meaning God's relationship with Israel expressed in the law and temple worship. The real battle line is not between North and South but between those who forsake the covenant and those who keep it.

Tsevi, beauty or glory, used in the phrase the Beautiful Land (verses 16, 41) for the land of Israel and the beautiful holy mountain (verse 45) for Zion. The land God gave is precious in his eyes even when it is trampled by armies.

christ: The chapter does not speak of the Messiah directly, but it prepares for him in two ways. First, it shows the pattern of the proud ruler who exalts himself above every god, and the New Testament uses this language for the opposition Christ will finally overthrow: Paul describes a man of lawlessness who exalts himself over every so-called god and whom the Lord Jesus will destroy by his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:3-8). Second, it shows faithful people suffering, teaching, and being refined while the powers rage. Jesus took up Daniel's language of the abomination of desolation (Matthew 24:15) and called his followers to endure; and many interpreters think the Maccabean martyrs who resisted Antiochus are among those Hebrews 11:35 honors for refusing release in hope of a better resurrection. The final answer to the king who magnifies himself is not a stronger king of the North or South, but the kingdom given to the Son of Man (7:13-14).

hard.q: Why is the history so precise, and who is the king of verses 36-45?
hard.a:
The precision of verses 2-35 is at the center of the debate over Daniel's date. The historical-critical view holds that the chapter was written during Antiochus IV's persecution, about 167 to 164 BC: the writer surveys past history in the form of prophecy, as other Jewish apocalypses did, so that readers see their crisis inside God's plan. Verses 40-45, which describe a final Egyptian campaign and a death between the sea and the holy mountain, do not match what is known of Antiochus's death in Persia in 164 BC, so these scholars read them as a genuine prediction written shortly before his death.

The traditional view holds that God revealed the history to Daniel in the sixth century BC, and that its precision shows God's knowledge of the future. Many who hold this view, following an approach found already in Jerome, see the text passing beyond Antiochus at some point (often at verse 36) to a final Antichrist, with Antiochus as a type or foreshadowing. The dispensational view holds the same traditional date and reads verses 36-45 as a future ruler in the last days before Christ's return, with the kings of the North and South as powers of that future time; it does not rely on identifying them with present-day nations.

Every view agrees on what the chapter asks of its readers: that the people who know their God should stand firm, teach others, and trust that the persecutor will meet his end with no one to help him.

questions: The chapter makes the wars of empires look repetitive and futile. What does that say about where lasting significance is found?
Antiochus corrupted many through flattery rather than force. Which is the greater danger to faith where you live: open pressure or quiet compromise?
The wise instruct many and some of them fall. Who taught you the faith at a cost to themselves, and what does it mean to do the same for someone else?
